title: Descending Control and the Basal Ganglia

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Codex accuracy gate → fixes

cards.front: To predict what a lesion or drug does to movement, you follow the motor chain toward the muscle and count two things. What does each count set?
cards.back: Midline crossings set the side: an odd number puts the effect on the opposite side. Inhibitory links set the sign: an even number keeps the direction of a change, an odd number reverses it.
cards.why: The counts give the side and direction of a change, not its size.
cards.quote: Each crossing of the midline flips the side: an odd number of crossings puts the effect on the opposite side of the body.

cards.front: What is an upper motor neuron?
cards.back: A neuron in the cortex or brainstem whose axon descends to control lower motor neurons, directly or through interneurons.
cards.quote: The line starts at an upper motor neuron: a neuron in the cortex or brainstem whose axon descends to control lower motor neurons, directly or through interneurons.

cards.front: A {{c1::lower motor neuron}} is a motor neuron in the brainstem or the spinal cord's ventral horn whose axon leaves the central nervous system and ends on muscle.
cards.quote: It ends at a lower motor neuron: a motor neuron in the brainstem or the spinal cord's ventral horn whose axon leaves the central nervous system and ends on muscle.

cards.front: A {{c1::decussation}} is a place where a tract crosses the midline.
cards.quote: The X is a decussation, a place where a tract crosses the midline.

cards.front: The corticospinal tract starts in layer V of primary motor cortex. Name, in order, the five stops its axons pass on the way to the medulla.
cards.back: Corona radiata; posterior limb of the internal capsule; cerebral peduncle of the midbrain; base of the pons; medullary pyramids.
cards.quote: the corona radiata; the posterior limb of the internal capsule; the cerebral peduncle of the midbrain; the base of the pons; the medullary pyramids

cards.front: Most corticospinal fibres cross the midline at the {{c1::pyramidal decussation}} in the caudal medulla.
cards.back: The crossed fibres then run in the lateral column of the cord as the lateral corticospinal tract.
cards.quote: In the caudal medulla most of the fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation.

cards.front: Why does a corticospinal lesion above the pyramidal decussation weaken the opposite side of the body, while a lesion in the spinal cord weakens the same side?
cards.back: Above the decussation one crossing still lies between the lesion and the muscle, so the effect is contralateral. In the cord the fibres have already crossed, so it is ipsilateral.
cards.quote: Damage above it, with one crossing still to come, shows up on the opposite side of the body.

cards.front: Why does a lower motor neuron lesion cause low tone and reduced or absent reflexes?
cards.back: The motor limb of the reflex arc is cut. Later the muscle wastes and may show fasciculations, visible twitches of single motor units firing on their own.
cards.quote: A lower motor neuron lesion causes weakness with low tone and reduced or absent reflexes, because the motor limb of the reflex arc is cut.
cards.section: Which neuron is damaged: the signs

cards.front: List the signs of an established upper motor neuron lesion.
cards.back: Weakness with raised tone, brisk stretch reflexes, clonus, and an extensor plantar response (the great toe extends when the sole is stroked). Independent finger movements are often lost.
cards.quote: An established upper motor neuron lesion causes weakness with raised tone (more resistance when the limb is moved passively), brisk stretch reflexes
cards.section: Which neuron is damaged: the signs

cards.front: One day after a cervical spinal cord injury, the limbs below the injury are flaccid and have no reflexes. Does this rule out damage to upper motor neuron axons?
cards.back: No. This is spinal shock; spasticity appears later.
cards.why: Upper motor neuron signs are read once established, weeks after onset. Right after a cord injury the limbs below can be flaccid and areflexic.
cards.quote: Right after a spinal cord injury the limbs below can be flaccid and areflexic (spinal shock), and spasticity appears later.
cards.section: Which neuron is damaged: the signs

cards.front: Why does an upper motor neuron lesion above the brainstem weaken the contralateral lower face more than the forehead?
cards.back: Corticobulbar input to lower-face motor neurons comes mainly from the opposite cortex, while the forehead receives input from both sides, so the forehead is relatively spared.
cards.quote: Corticobulbar fibres to the motor neurons for the lower face come mainly from the opposite cortex, while the forehead receives input from both sides.
cards.section: Which neuron is damaged: the signs

cards.front: Weeks after one focal lesion, a patient has weakness of the right lower face, right arm and right leg, with raised tone, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response on the right. Where is the lesion most likely?
cards.back: The left hemisphere, for example the posterior limb of the left internal capsule.
cards.why: Upper motor neuron signs put it in the descending pathway. Lower-face weakness puts it above the facial nucleus. Above the decussation the deficit is contralateral.
cards.quote: most likely the left hemisphere, for example the posterior limb of the left internal capsule, where descending fibres for the face, arm and leg are packed

cards.front: Where does the dorsal column pathway (touch, vibration) cross the midline, and where does the spinothalamic pathway (pain, temperature) cross?
cards.back: Dorsal column: in the medulla. Spinothalamic: within a segment or two of entering the cord.
cards.quote: The dorsal column pathway for touch and vibration crosses in the medulla; the spinothalamic pathway for pain and temperature crosses within a segment or two of entering the cord

cards.front: One lesion destroys the left half of the spinal cord at a mid-thoracic level. On which side would you expect leg weakness with upper motor neuron signs, vibration loss, and pain and temperature loss?
cards.back: Leg weakness and vibration loss on the left; pain and temperature loss on the right, starting a little below the lesion.
cards.why: In the cord, corticospinal and spinothalamic fibres have already crossed; dorsal column fibres have not.
cards.quote: The dorsal columns have not yet crossed in the cord, so right vibration loss points to the right cord.

cards.front: In a right hemisection of the cervical cord near C5, why are lower motor neuron signs expected at the level of the lesion itself?
cards.back: Ventral horn cells at that level are destroyed. Below the level, the cut descending axons give upper motor neuron signs.
cards.quote: with lower motor neuron signs expected at the level itself, where ventral horn cells are destroyed

cards.front: In the classic model of the basal ganglia, which structure is the input stage and which is the output stage?
cards.back: Input: the striatum (caudate and putamen). Output: the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi), with its partner the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
cards.quote: The output stage is the internal segment of the globus pallidus, GPi, with a partner that works much the same way
cards.section: Counting inhibitions: the basal ganglia brake

cards.front: Why is the motor thalamus under steady inhibition at rest, and what must happen for movement in the classic model?
cards.back: GPi and SNr output neurons are GABAergic and fire tonically, even at rest, like a foot on a brake. Movement needs the brake lifted: GPi must fire less.
cards.quote: The output neurons of GPi and SNr are GABAergic, releasing the inhibitory transmitter GABA, and fire tonically, that is, steadily, even at rest.

cards.front: What is disinhibition, and what condition must hold for it to pass a change on?
cards.back: Inhibiting an inhibitor releases its target: two inhibitory links in a row keep the direction of a change. Each cell must still be able to change its firing.
cards.why: Removing inhibition only permits firing; the target's own excitatory drive does the exciting.
cards.quote: two inhibitory links in a row pass the change on with its direction kept, as long as each cell can still change its firing

cards.front: Neuron A inhibits B, and B inhibits C, which has steady excitatory drive of its own. B is already silent. A starts firing faster. What does C do?
cards.back: Nothing changes. B cannot slow further, so C's inhibition does not fall.
cards.why: Disinhibition passes a change on only while each cell in the chain can still change its firing.
cards.quote: a B that is already silent cannot slow further

cards.front: Give the indirect basal ganglia pathway from striatum to thalamus, with the sign of each link.
cards.back: Striatum (D2 neurons) ⊣ GPe ⊣ STN → GPi ⊣ thalamus. STN is glutamatergic and excites GPi; the other links are GABAergic.
cards.quote: In the indirect pathway, striatal neurons that express D2 receptors inhibit GPe; GPe, also GABAergic, inhibits STN;

cards.front: In the classic rate model, why does more striatal firing in the direct pathway push toward movement, and more in the indirect pathway push away?
cards.back: Direct (striatum ⊣ GPi ⊣ thalamus): two inhibitions, even, so the thalamus is released. Indirect: three inhibitions, odd, so the thalamus is held down harder.
cards.quote: A released thalamus means a push toward movement; a thalamus held down harder means a push away.

cards.front: Give each excitatory link +1 and each inhibitory link −1. Compute the sign product of the indirect loop: cortex → striatum ⊣ GPe ⊣ STN → GPi ⊣ thalamus → cortex. What does the sign mean?
cards.back: (+1)(−1)(−1)(+1)(−1)(+1) = −1. Negative: activity entering the loop ends up holding the thalamus down, against movement.
cards.quote: a negative product means it ends up holding the thalamus down
cards.section: The count as a product of signs

cards.front: In the classic rate model, striatal D2 neurons are driven to fire faster. Predict GPe, STN, GPi, the thalamus and movement.
cards.back: GPe fires less; STN, freed from GPe, fires more; GPi, excited by STN, fires more; the thalamus is held down harder, away from movement.
cards.quote: D2 neurons fire more, so GPe fires less. STN, freed from GPe, fires more. GPi, excited by STN, fires more.

cards.front: In the classic rate model, how does dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) act on each striatal projection population?
cards.back: It excites D1 direct-pathway neurons and inhibits D2 indirect-pathway neurons.
cards.quote: it excites D1 direct-pathway neurons and inhibits D2 indirect-pathway neurons

cards.front: Count the sign flips to show that dopamine acting through D2 receptors pushes toward movement in the classic model.
cards.back: Dopamine's inhibition of D2 neurons is one flip, then the indirect route's three inhibitions: four flips, even, so more dopamine means more movement.
cards.quote: Through D2: dopamine's inhibitory action is one flip, then the indirect route's three.

cards.front: In the classic rate model, SNc dopamine neurons are lost. Predict GPi firing, the thalamus and movement.
cards.back: GPi fires more, the thalamus is held down harder, and movement becomes hard to start (akinesia).
cards.why: Two reasons at once: the weakened direct pathway inhibits GPi less, and the strengthened indirect pathway releases STN, which excites GPi more.
cards.quote: So GPi fires more for two reasons at once: less inhibition from the striatum, and more excitation from STN.

cards.front: When can the inhibition count predict a net effect, and when can it not?
cards.back: It can when all the routes carrying a change agree in sign. When they disagree it says only that they pull against each other; which wins depends on route strength.
cards.quote: When several routes carry a change and agree in sign, the count predicts the net effect.

cards.front: In a hypothetical MPTP experiment (numbers invented), mean STN firing rises from 20 to 30 spikes per second and GPi firing from 70 to 98 spikes per second. Give each percent change and say whether the directions fit the classic rate model.
cards.back: STN: 10/20 = +50%. GPi: 28/70 = +40%. Both rises fit the model's prediction for dopamine loss.
cards.why: Dopamine loss strengthens the indirect pathway, releasing STN, which drives GPi. The count predicts direction, not size.
cards.quote: The direct pathway weakens and the indirect pathway strengthens: GPe is more inhibited and STN is released.

cards.front: A monkey made parkinsonian with MPTP receives a lesion of the right subthalamic nucleus (STN). Which way should movement change, and on which side of the body?
cards.back: Parkinsonian signs should ease on the left side.
cards.why: Sign: STN → GPi ⊣ thalamus has one inhibition, so less STN activity releases the thalamus. Side: the right loop returns to right cortex, whose commands cross once.
cards.quote: Left STN, left GPi, left thalamus, left cortex, then one crossing on the way to the cord: the right side of the body.
cards.section: Both counts together: silencing the STN

cards.front: In MPTP-treated monkeys, one STN was lesioned (reported in 1990). What happened to the parkinsonian signs, and why did the result matter?
cards.back: They improved on the side of the body opposite the lesion. A testable rate-model prediction held, and the STN became a surgical target.
cards.quote: reported in Science in 1990 that the parkinsonian signs improved on the side of the body opposite the lesion
cards.section: Both counts together: silencing the STN

cards.front: A person without Parkinson's disease has a small stroke in the left STN. Predict the movement change and its side.
cards.back: A left STN stroke can cause hemiballism: large flinging movements of the right arm or leg.
cards.why: Reduced STN excitation of GPi releases the thalamus; with normal dopamine this can release movement too far. One crossing places the effect on the right.
cards.quote: A lesion in or near one STN, classically a small stroke in a person without Parkinson's disease, can release the opposite limbs too far.
cards.section: Both counts together: silencing the STN

cards.front: In the classic rate model, a drug blocks dopamine's action on D2 receptors in the left striatum only. Predict the change in movement and the side of the body affected.
cards.back: Less movement, on the right side.
cards.why: Rests on dopamine inhibiting D2 neurons: blocking it lets them fire more, so GPe falls, STN and GPi rise, and the left thalamus is held down. The left loop's cortical commands cross once.
cards.quote: In the classic model each hemisphere's basal ganglia loop returns to the cortex on its own side, and that cortex's commands cross once, at the pyramidal decussation.
cards.section: Both counts together: silencing the STN

cards.front: How does L-DOPA treat Parkinson's disease?
cards.back: It is a dopamine precursor that raises the dopamine available in the striatum.
cards.quote: A dopamine precursor such as L-DOPA raises the dopamine available in the striatum.
cards.section: Parkinson's and Huntington's through the circuit

cards.front: Mice are depleted of dopamine with 6-hydroxydopamine. Driving direct-pathway striatal neurons with light rescues their motor deficits. How does the rate model account for this?
cards.back: Dopamine loss weakens the direct pathway. Driving those neurons restores its two-inhibition route that releases the thalamus, standing in for the missing dopamine excitation of D1 neurons.
cards.quote: In mice with dopamine depleted by 6-hydroxydopamine, driving direct-pathway neurons with light rescued the motor deficits Kravitz and colleagues measured (2010).
cards.section: Parkinson's and Huntington's through the circuit

cards.front: What causes Huntington's disease, and is it a primary loss of dopamine?
cards.back: An expanded CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene. It is not a primary loss of dopamine.
cards.quote: an expanded CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene (the mutation type is in mutation), not a primary loss of dopamine
cards.section: Parkinson's and Huntington's through the circuit

cards.front: In the classic rate model, striatal neurons that project to GPe lose their output first, as thought to happen in early Huntington's disease. Predict GPe, STN, GPi, the thalamus and movement.
cards.back: GPe is released and fires more; STN is more inhibited and fires less; GPi gets less excitation and fires less; the thalamus is released, pushing toward extra movement (chorea).
cards.quote: Losing that output removes the inhibition of GPe, so GPe is released and fires more.
cards.section: Parkinson's and Huntington's through the circuit

cards.front: Enkephalin marks the striatal projection to GPe and substance P the projection to GPi. In post-mortem tissue from early Huntington's disease, GPe enkephalin terminals are more affected. What does this support, and what can it not show?
cards.back: It supports the premise that the GPe-projecting (indirect) output is affected first. Staining alone cannot tell neuron death from terminal loss or reduced peptide.
cards.quote: Staining alone cannot tell neuron death from terminal loss or reduced peptide.
cards.section: Parkinson's and Huntington's through the circuit

cards.front: Parkinson's disease and early Huntington's disease both damage the basal ganglia, yet push movement in opposite directions. Using the rate model, explain why.
cards.back: Parkinson's: dopamine loss weakens the direct and strengthens the indirect route, so GPi rises, the thalamus is held down: akinesia. Early Huntington's: GPe-projecting output falls, so GPe rises, STN and GPi fall, the thalamus is released: extra movement.
cards.why: The inhibition count along each route sets the sign of GPi's change, and GPi's change sets the thalamus's.
cards.quote: GPi gets less excitation and fires less, and the thalamus is released.
cards.section: Parkinson's and Huntington's through the circuit

cards.front: In mice, calcium signals from both direct-pathway (D1) and indirect-pathway (A2A) striatal neurons rise around the start of an action. Why does this challenge the classic rate model?
cards.back: The model has the pathways alternating. Two routes of opposite sign active together is exactly the case the sign count cannot call.
cards.quote: Two routes of opposite sign active at once is exactly the case the count cannot call.

cards.front: Cortical stimulation evokes an early, STN-dependent excitation of the pallidum: the hyperdirect pathway, cortex → STN → GPi ⊣ thalamus. Count its signs. Does cortical drive through it push toward or away from movement?
cards.back: One inhibition, odd: away from movement, against the direct route.
cards.quote: One inhibition, so it pushes away from movement, against the direct route.

cards.front: In mice, direct-pathway striatal neurons also branch into GPe. With simple signs, what should inhibiting those GPe terminals do to motor performance, and what was found?
cards.back: The count predicts better performance, since the branch through GPe and STN has three inhibitions and opposes the direct route. Instead performance was impaired, partly through Npas1-expressing GPe neurons, so the count cannot sign this branch.
cards.quote: Yet inhibiting the direct-pathway terminals in GPe impaired the mice's motor performance, the opposite of what that count predicts.

cards.front: Besides mean firing rate, what changes in parkinsonian basal ganglia that the classic rate model leaves out?
cards.back: Firing pattern: more bursting and synchronized oscillation in STN and GPi, and, in dopamine-depleted mice, disrupted clustering of indirect-pathway activity.
cards.quote: Studies of parkinsonian animals and patients also report more bursting and synchronized oscillation in STN and GPi.

cards.front: Use the rate model to predict two effects of lesioning GPi (pallidotomy) in Parkinson's disease. Which prediction fails?
cards.back: Relief of parkinsonism, since the thalamus is released: this holds. Extra movements from removing GPi output: this fails. Pallidotomy usually does not cause them and also eases dyskinesia and dystonia.
cards.quote: But the model also predicts that removing GPi output should cause extra movements, and pallidotomy usually does not cause them

cards.front: Name two features of Parkinson's disease and its treatment that the classic rate model does not explain.
cards.back: Rest tremor, and how deep brain stimulation of the STN relieves parkinsonian signs.
cards.quote: The model gives no account of rest tremor, and deep brain stimulation of the STN relieves parkinsonian signs by a mechanism that is still unresolved.

cards.front: Design a primate experiment to test whether silencing an overactive STN relieves parkinsonism by lowering GPi firing, as the rate model says. What results would count against the model?
cards.back: MPTP monkeys; record STN and GPi before and after MPTP (both should rise). Lesion one STN and score akinesia and rigidity on the opposite side, the other side as comparison. Controls: sham surgery, histology, blind scoring, GPi recording after the lesion. Against: no improvement after an accurate lesion, or improvement with no fall in GPi.
cards.why: Pattern and synchrony change too, so record them; a lesion result does not explain deep brain stimulation.
cards.quote: or improvement with no fall in GPi activity, which would mean the benefit does not work by lowering GPi rate as the model says

cards.front: Of 148 direct-pathway neurons in mouse dorsomedial striatum that carried an SNr tracer, 147 also carried a GPe tracer. What percentage is that, and of which population?
cards.back: 147/148 = 99.3% of the SNr-labelled cells counted, not of all striatal neurons.
cards.quote: That is 147/148 = 99.3% of the SNr-labelled cells counted, not of all striatal neurons.
